title: Explain slaughter procedures and related animal welfare concerns

lessons.title: Categories of slaughter, the law and abattoir species
lessons.html:
Categories of slaughter

Animals are slaughtered in South Africa in several different settings. Each has its own rules and welfare risks.

  • Commercial slaughter at a registered abattoir, where meat is inspected and sold to the public.
  • Religious slaughter, such as halaal and kosher slaughter, done according to religious rules, usually in abattoirs registered for that purpose.
  • Traditional or cultural slaughter, for example a goat or ox slaughtered at home for a ceremony.
  • Slaughter for own consumption on the farm, where the meat is not sold.
  • Emergency slaughter of an injured animal that is fit to be eaten, and killing for disease control, where carcasses are destroyed, not eaten.

Legislation

  • Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000: requires animals slaughtered for meat for sale to be slaughtered at a registered abattoir, with ante-mortem and post-mortem inspection, and sets hygiene and humane slaughter standards. It allows for slaughter for own consumption and for religious or cultural purposes under conditions.
  • Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962: applies everywhere, including at home and at the abattoir. Causing unnecessary suffering during handling, transport or killing is an offence.
  • Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984: controls movement and slaughter linked to disease control.

Industry codes and the Meat Safety Act regulations require trained operators, correct stunning equipment and calm handling in lairages.

Species slaughtered in abattoirs

TypeSpecies
Red meatCattle, sheep, goats, pigs, horses (for export and other markets)
White meatChickens, ducks, turkeys, ostriches (handled in ostrich abattoirs)
OtherGame species, rabbits, crocodiles in specialised facilities

Some carcasses or animals are slaughtered for non-human use, such as pet food or animal feed. These must be kept separate and clearly marked so that they never enter the human food chain.

lessons.title: The slaughter process in red and white meat abattoirs
lessons.html:
Red meat abattoirs

  1. Arrival and lairage: animals are offloaded calmly and rested in pens with water. Injured animals are identified at once.
  2. Ante-mortem inspection: a meat inspector checks animals for disease, injury and fitness for slaughter.
  3. Moving to the stunning box: along a race without shouting, sticks or electric prodders used carelessly.
  4. Stunning: cattle are usually stunned with a penetrating captive bolt; sheep and pigs often with electrical head-only stunning. The animal must be unconscious immediately.
  5. Shackling and bleeding (sticking): the main blood vessels are cut quickly after stunning so that the animal dies before it can regain consciousness.
  6. Dressing: removing the head, feet and hide, then evisceration (removing the organs).
  7. Post-mortem inspection of carcass and organs, then splitting, washing, classification and chilling.

Welfare checkpoints

  • Short time from stun to stick.
  • Check every animal for signs of consciousness after stunning: rhythmic breathing, blinking when the eye is touched, trying to lift the head, or vocalising. If seen, re-stun immediately.
  • Equipment maintained and a back-up stunner ready.

White meat abattoirs

  1. Receiving: crates of birds are kept in shade with ventilation. Dead-on-arrival birds are counted.
  2. Shackling: live birds are hung by the legs gently. Rough shackling causes broken legs and bruising.
  3. Stunning: most often an electrical water-bath, sometimes controlled-atmosphere systems.
  4. Neck cutting and bleeding, by machine with a back-up person to catch missed birds.
  5. Scalding and plucking, then evisceration, inspection and chilling in air or water.
  6. Portioning and packing.

A bird must never enter the scald tank alive. The back-up operator is the key welfare safeguard.

Key points

  • Slaughter categories include commercial, religious, cultural, own consumption and emergency slaughter.
  • Meat for sale must come from a registered abattoir under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000.
  • The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 applies to all slaughter.
  • Stunning must cause immediate unconsciousness, followed quickly by bleeding.
  • Check for signs of consciousness and re-stun at once if needed.
